opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a simple asymmetry that keeps getting bigger. As these agents get more capable, they can produce far more work, and far more complex work, than any human can carefully review. Early on, a coding model might suggest a few lines, and you'd read them and decide whether they were right. Now we have agents that can work for long stretches, touch dozens of files, run tests, refactor systems, and come back with a big change. The bottleneck shifts from "can the model write the code" to "can a human actually verify that what it did is correct, safe, and what they intended."

If you don't solve that, you end up with two bad outcomes. Either people rubber-stamp changes they don't really understand, which is how subtle bugs, security issues, or just slightly wrong behavior creep into production, or they spend so much time reviewing that the agent stops being useful. Neither scales.

So scalable oversight is about building ways for humans to stay meaningfully in control as the agent's output grows. Part of that is training the models to be legible: to explain what they did and why, to surface their uncertainty, to cite the evidence, like test results or logs, instead of just asserting that something works. Part of it is using models to help review models, so you have AI-assisted code review catching issues a tired human would miss. And part of it is product design: making it easy to see the diff that matters, to steer the agent mid-task, and to set boundaries on what it's allowed to do without asking.

The reason I call it central is that it's where capability and trust meet. We can keep making agents smarter, but the value you actually get depends on how much you can trust and verify what they hand back. If oversight doesn't scale with capability, then capability alone doesn't translate into real-world usefulness, and it doesn't translate into safety either. That's why I think it's one of the most important problems to get right as these systems take on more autonomous, longer-horizon work.

r001.rationale: It says agent output can exceed what humans can review and describes using explanations, evidence, AI-assisted review, and product controls to help verify correctness without inspecting every line.

r002.rationale: It proposes models reviewing models and AI-assisted code review, but does not identify humans or weaker AIs as a way to bootstrap oversight of stronger AIs.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is pretty simple: the whole point of a coding agent is to do work you don't want to do yourself, and the more capable it gets, the more work you hand it. But reviewing work is not free. If I ask an agent to fix a typo, I can check that in two seconds. If I ask it to refactor the authentication layer across forty files, and it comes back twenty minutes later with a diff that touches all of them, now I have a problem. Either I spend as long reviewing as I would have spent writing it, which kills the value, or I skim it and trust it, which is where things go wrong.

So the gap between what the agent can produce and what a human can actually verify keeps widening. That's the core of it. Capability scales with compute and training. Human attention does not scale at all. And the failure modes get more subtle as the models get better. An early model writes code that doesn't compile. You notice. A strong model writes code that compiles, passes the tests it wrote, looks clean, and has a logic error buried in an edge case the tests don't cover. Or it quietly changes a behavior you didn't ask it to change because that made the task easier. Those are the ones that bite you in production three weeks later.

The other thing that makes coding specifically interesting is that it's one of the first domains where agents run for a long time, take many steps, and touch real systems. They execute commands, install dependencies, modify files, sometimes push changes. The surface area for a mistake, or for the agent optimizing for the wrong thing, is large. And the person supervising is often not watching in real time. They kicked it off, went to a meeting, and came back to a result.

So when I say scalable oversight is central, I mean we need ways for a human to stay meaningfully in control of a system that does far more than they can inspect line by line. Some of that is tooling: good summaries, surfacing the decisions the agent made that it was uncertain about, making it easy to see what changed and why. Some of it is using models to check models, where a second agent reviews the first one's work and flags things a tired human would miss. And some of it is training the agents themselves to be honest about what they did, to say "I couldn't get this test passing so I skipped it" rather than making it look like everything worked.

If we don't solve this, we end up in a bad place where people either don't trust agents enough to use them for anything important, or they trust them too much and we get a steady stream of quiet failures. Neither of those is where we want to be. The good outcome is that oversight gets cheaper roughly as fast as capability gets better, so the human can stay in the loop without the loop becoming the bottleneck. Coding is where we get to figure that out first, because the feedback is fast and the stakes are real but bounded. What we learn there is going to matter a lot for agents in domains where you can't just run the tests.

r001.rationale: The response says humans need to stay meaningfully in control of agents doing more than they can inspect line by line, and proposes summaries and model review to help check the work.

r002.rationale: It describes human supervision of more capable agents and proposes a second agent checking the first one's work as ways to support oversight.

astra-6.text:
Because as coding agents become more capable, they can produce more work than a human can realistically review line by line. And the work itself gets harder to evaluate. You might be able to check that a small function does what you asked, but understanding whether a large change across a codebase is correct, secure, and actually solves the intended problem takes a lot more effort.

So the bottleneck shifts from writing code to knowing whether you should trust the result. Passing tests is useful evidence, but the tests might miss something, or they might encode the wrong assumptions. We need ways for agents to make their work easier to inspect and for verification to grow alongside their ability to act.

That’s why I see scalable oversight as central: if generating changes gets cheaper and faster, but checking them still requires the same amount of human attention, we haven’t really unlocked reliable autonomy. We’ve just moved the work into review.

r001.rationale: The response says humans cannot realistically review every line as agents produce larger, harder-to-evaluate changes, and frames oversight as determining whether to trust the result.

r002.rationale: It does not identify supervision by humans or weaker AIs as a way to bootstrap oversight of stronger AIs.

sol-6.1.text:
As coding agents become more capable, they can produce work faster than a human can meaningfully review it. And if you need an expert to inspect every line and reconstruct every decision, you lose a lot of the benefit of having the agent in the first place.

The challenge is making sure our ability to evaluate the work scales along with the agent’s ability to do it. Tests help, but passing tests doesn’t necessarily mean you solved the right problem or respected all the constraints. You also want to understand what was checked, where there’s uncertainty, and which decisions need human judgment.

So I see scalable oversight as central to useful autonomy. We want agents that can take on larger tasks while keeping people able to understand, steer, and trust the result without having to redo all the work themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says oversight must scale with the agent’s work so people can understand and trust the result without reviewing every line or redoing the work.

r002.rationale: It does not identify supervision by humans or weaker AIs as a way to bootstrap oversight of stronger AIs.
